hero.kicker: Can you predict where New York wants a ride tomorrow?
hero.cap: lower error than a simple guess.
hero.fine: That is the LightGBM model I trained, forecasting ride demand in each of 30 New York zones, a day ahead. A simple guess averages what happened at that hour on that weekday over the last 4 weeks: for next Tuesday at 6pm, the last four Tuesdays at 6pm. Tested on 28 days it never saw, scored once.

hero_compact.kicker: Dashboard: pick a zone and a day, the headline stays up here

verdict: The model won on 26 of 28 held-out days. Its largest miss, a winter storm, was in the development period, before the held-out test.
plain: When you open a ride-hailing app, a car is usually already nearby. That is because someone guessed, ahead of time, how many people would want a ride in each part of the city that hour. This project makes that guess.
It predicts, a day ahead and hour by hour, how many ride requests each of 30 parts of New York will get. It learns from real trip records published by the city's Taxi and Limousine Commission.

To check it honestly, I hid the last 4 weeks of data and made the model forecast each of those days before seeing what happened. Its guesses were off by about 31 rides per zone per hour. A simple guess was off by about 36: to guess next Tuesday at 6pm, it just averages the last four Tuesdays at 6pm. That is 14% fewer misses.
In the busiest zone (Queens, LaGuardia Airport), the model missed by about 115 rides an hour against 123 for the simple guess.

It has one big blind spot: the weather. The worst day was 25 January, in the development period, before the held-out test (cause: Major winter storm), when its average miss was 4.9 times a typical day's. The model cannot see the weather, so a storm like that catches it out. The Storm days tab in the dashboard has the details.

up_close.takeaway: Wed 30 Sep: About the same as the simple rule (100.3 against 103.0 rides an hour). The model's biggest miss was at 19:00, when it forecast 912 and 1235 rides actually happened.
up_close.note: This day was picked by rule, not because it looks good: the busiest zone, on the last day tested.

glossary: The simple guess the model has to beat. Here: to forecast next Tuesday at 6pm, average the last four Tuesdays at 6pm.
Mean absolute error: how many rides the forecast was off by, on average, in one zone in one hour. Lower is better.
Data the model never saw while it was being built, saved for one final test so the result cannot be flattered.
Replaying the past: pretend it is midnight on some past day, forecast the next 24 hours, then compare with what happened.
The yellow band on the charts: the range the model expected most hours to land in. It is not a promise.
One of New York's taxi zones, the neighbourhood-sized areas the city uses for trip records.

findings.lab: Fewer misses than the simple rule
findings.sub: Average miss 31.38 against 36.37 rides per zone per hour, on 28 held-out days the model never saw.

findings.lab: A classic statistical model vs the simple rule
findings.sub: Fancier did not mean better. Mixing the main model back toward the simple rule did worse than LightGBM alone.

findings.lab: Major winter storm on 25 Jan (development period): storms still fool it
findings.sub: the median daily error. Nothing in the model knows the weather.

mind.title: It beats the simple rule in most zones
mind.detail: It beat the rule in 28 of 30 zones.

mind.title: The gain is not just the busiest zone
mind.detail: With the busiest zone removed, the model still made 14.6% fewer misses than the rule.

mind.title: It wins on most days, not a few lucky ones
mind.detail: It beat the rule on 26 of 28 held-out days.

mind.title: The yellow band can be trusted
mind.detail: The 10 to 90% band caught 75% of held-out hours before rounding, and 82% after its edges were rounded out to whole trips; an ideal band catches 80%.

mind.title: It keeps winning in another month or year
mind.detail: Only one month was held out, and I have one year of history. I cannot rule this out.

evidence.title: Demand and ETR Forecasting at Airports
evidence.why: Uber's own airports team forecasts demand because too few drivers means riders struggle to get a ride, and too many means drivers sit idle.

evidence.title: Taxi and Limousine Commission passes new rules protecting app drivers from lockouts
evidence.why: New York's regulator voted rules on when apps may cut off driver access, after drivers alleged lockouts lowered their pay. How many drivers work, and when, is a live issue in this city.
evidence.credit: Image: AP file photo, via NY1

evidence.title: Real-Time Spatial Temporal Forecasting @ Lyft
evidence.why: Lyft's engineers describe forecasts behind decisions from real-time rider pricing and driver incentives to budget planning, and look at how simple classical time-series models do the job in real time.

steps.sub: Every day at 00:00 the model forecasts the next 24 hours using only data before that moment.
A leak test recomputes every feature from raw history. It was shown to catch three deliberately planted leaks.
Four simple rules were scored by the same code before any model, so a model has to earn its place.
The last 4 weeks were set aside until every choice was frozen, then scored 1 time.

next_steps.sub: The model cannot see the weather, and storms change how many people want a ride. Feeding in a forecast is the obvious next step.
One year means every holiday appears once. Two or three years would let the model learn them properly.
30 zones were checked. The honest next test is every zone in the city, and a different month of held-out days.
The same testing code can be pointed at a different forecasting problem, such as electricity demand, to see if the approach holds.

fleet.intro: An example of how this work could move into a real ride-hail company. The middle column is a plan, not something I have built.

columns.title: What carries over
items: The backtest harness: forecast each day using only what was known before it, then move forward one day.
The leak test, shown to fail on three deliberately planted leaks.
Simple baselines scored first, so a model has to beat them to count.
A held-out period scored once, with every number on this site read from a results file.

columns.title: What would change
items: Their own demand and supply data instead of public trip records.
Weather, events and prices as inputs. Storm days, all in the development period, were the largest errors here.
Finer zones, and a rule for brand-new zones with no history.
A forecast with a range, scored on what a wrong forecast costs dispatch, not only on average error.
Monitoring to catch the model drifting after launch.

columns.title: What this does not prove
items: Only one month was held out, from one year of history.
There is no weather or event input.
The data is public trip records, not a company's live requests.
It was never tested against a running system.
